vo_open.text: Seven deep-sea creatures that look fake.
All of them are real. And number one might be older than the United States.

vo.text: Number seven. The pistol shrimp.
It snaps its giant claw shut so fast that it fires a bubble, at ninety kilometers per hour.
vo.cap: It fires a bubble at *90 km/h.*

vo.text: When that bubble collapses, it makes a sound of two hundred eighteen decibels underwater. Enough to stun a fish.
vo.cap: *218 dB* underwater. Enough to *stun a fish.*

vo.text: The bubble even gives off a flash of light. Glowing like that would take over five thousand kelvin. Close to the surface of the Sun.
vo.cap: Over *5,000 K.* The Sun's surface: *5,772 K.*

vo.text: And when a whole colony snaps at once, it's loud enough to interfere with sonar.
Some live with a goby. The fish keeps watch, while the shrimp keeps one antenna on it.
And one species was named after Pink Floyd, because of its bright pink claw.
Number six. The tongue-eating louse.
Look inside this fish's mouth. That's not its tongue. It's a parasite.
vo.cap: That's not a tongue. It's a *parasite.*

vo.text: It gets in through the gills while it's young, and grabs onto the tongue.
Then it cuts off the blood supply, until the tongue falls off.
vo.cap: It cuts the *blood supply.* The tongue *falls off.*

vo.text: And it takes its place. The fish keeps using it, like a real tongue.
vo.cap: The fish uses it like a *real tongue.*

vo.text: Even stranger: if a second male moves into the same fish, the first male turns into a female.
Females are only one to three centimeters long. And no, it's not harmful to humans.
Number five. The black seadevil.
It lives two hundred to fifteen hundred meters down, where sunlight never reaches.
So it makes its own light. The lure on its head glows, thanks to bacteria living inside it.
Its stomach stretches so much that it can eat a meal heavier than itself.
Females grow to about fifteen centimeters. Males stay under three.
Then, in February 2025, a living one was filmed at the surface, in daylight, off Tenerife.
Number four. The giant oarfish.
Quick favor: if you've learned something so far, subscribe. It really helps this tiny channel.
It's the longest bony fish alive. Seven to eight meters, maybe even more.
And it swims standing upright, tail down, rippling the long fin on its back.
Healthy ones are almost never seen. Most are found sick, or washed up on a beach.
This one washed up in Bermuda in 1860. Sixteen feet long. People called it a sea serpent.
In Japan, it's called the earthquake fish. Many washed up before the 2011 earthquake. But a 2019 study called the link an illusion.
Number three. The goblin shark.
Its lineage is about a hundred twenty-five million years old. Scientists call it a living fossil.
Its name comes from Japan: tenguzame, after the tengu, a goblin with a long nose.
When it bites, its jaws shoot forward, almost to the end of its snout.
And it's pink, because you can see the blood vessels under its skin.
vo.cap: Pink, from *blood vessels* under the skin.

vo.text: In 2023, a pregnant female caught off Taiwan was four point seven meters long, and weighed eight hundred kilos.
Number two. The colossal squid.
It has the biggest eyes of any known animal, ever. Up to thirty centimeters across. Bigger than a football.
vo.cap: Eyes up to *30 cm.* Bigger than a *football.*

vo.text: The heaviest one ever caught weighed four hundred ninety-five kilos. It's now on display in New Zealand.
Its arms and tentacles carry hooks. Some of them can swivel.
Sperm whales hunt them. In the Antarctic, fourteen percent of the squid beaks in their stomachs are colossal squid.
vo.cap: *14%* of the beaks in sperm whales.

vo.text: And nobody filmed a living one until March 2025. It was a baby, about thirty centimeters long.
And number one. The Greenland shark.
Scientists dated one using the lens of its eye. Three hundred ninety-two years old, give or take a hundred twenty. It was likely born before the United States existed.
It grows about one centimeter a year, and only becomes an adult at around a hundred fifty.
It's also incredibly slow. It cruises at about a third of a meter per second.
It can reach six point four meters, and more than a tonne.
Many are almost blind. A parasite hangs from their eyes.
Yet in their stomachs, scientists have found reindeer, moose, even polar bear.
Its meat is toxic. In Iceland, it's fermented and dried into a dish called hákarl.
So, seven creatures. Which one is the creepiest?
Comment its number. I read every single comment. And subscribe for more.

cta.q: Which one is the creepiest? Comment its number
